classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught multiplication by 100 to each decimal, retaining decimal digits or percentages above 100 where needed.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses decimal-to-percentage conversion.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 Example 1 converts decimals by multiplying by 100%; 100% equals one.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct decimal-to-percentage conversions, including values above one and small decimals.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct percentage-to-decimal conversion with decimal percentages.

questions.mappingNote: Each part reverses the notation conversion shown on page 1.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 defines percent as a fraction of 100 and shows 37%=37/100=0.37. Divide the percentage number by 100.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct percentage-to-decimal conversion with decimal percentages.

classification.difficultyReason: Write each percentage over 100, clear decimal numerators and simplify using common factors; the conversion method is supplied by teaching.

questions.mappingNote: The requested output is a fully simplified fraction; each part assesses conversion rather than percentage-of-quantity calculation.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of percent as a fraction of 100, clear any decimal numerator, then simplify.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert percentages to fractions and simplify, including small decimal percentages.

classification.difficultyReason: Multiply each fraction by 100 and simplify, retaining an exact mixed-number percentage for non-terminating results as taught.

questions.mappingNote: All fifteen parts directly assess fraction-to-percentage conversion. Parts m–o follow the exact-answer convention of Example 2(c).
questions.methodNote: Example 2 on pages 1–2 multiplies fractions by 100% and retains an exact mixed-number percentage for 1/11.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert fractions to percentages, retaining exact mixed-number percentages for recurring results.

classification.difficultyReason: Express quantities as percentages, converting time and length to matching units where necessary.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b match Example 3(a); parts c–d match Example 3(b); parts e–f apply the same matching-units method to lengths.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 Example 3 expresses a score as obtained/maximum times 100%, and converts minutes to seconds before forming a percentage.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express quantities as percentages, converting time and length to matching units where necessary.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct percentage calculations with whole-number and decimal percentages.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly asks for a percentage of a quantity, matching percentage-of-quantity. Part c follows Example 5 Method 1; the remaining worked answers use its exact fraction multiplication method.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 Example 5 teaches finding simple percentages from familiar percentage components and multiplying the quantity by the percentage expressed as a fraction of 100. Decimal multiplication is also demonstrated. Page 1 defines percent as a fraction of 100; page 2 demonstrates fraction-to-percentage conversions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct percentage calculations with whole-number and decimal percentages.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the percentage-of-a-quantity method when the quantity itself is a percentage, keeping the result in percentage units.

questions.mappingNote: Each part applies the taught percentage-of-a-quantity method to a quantity already expressed as a percentage, retaining the percentage unit in the result.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 defines percentages as fractions of 100. Page 2 demonstrates percentage conversions. Page 3, Example 5 Method 2, calculates a percentage of a quantity by multiplying by the percentage divided by 100.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct percentage calculations with results expressed as percentages.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct percentage calculations using the taught decimal multiplier method; calculator use is permitted.

questions.mappingNote: Each of parts a–f directly applies the page 3 calculator method: 0.13×20.5, 0.245×54.2, 0.013×32, 0.009×1100, 0.00032×1245 and 0.0105×32 respectively. All products terminate exactly, so no rounding instruction is needed.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 establishes percentages as fractions of 100. Page 3 Example 5 Method 2 and the calculator demonstration convert the percentage to a decimal and multiply by the quantity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct percentage calculations using the taught decimal multiplier method; calculator use is permitted.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate two familiar percentages using quarters and fifths, then observe that the numerical results are equal; no general proof is required.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (b) directly assess finding a percentage of a quantity. Part (c) compares those results; it does not yet require the general commutative proof requested by the following source question.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 defines percentages as fractions of 100; page 2 demonstrates fraction–percentage equivalence. Page 3 Example 5 prefers easily handled percentage calculations without a calculator and also supplies the fraction-times-quantity method. Use one quarter and one fifth for the two calculations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate two simple percentages and recognise that their results agree.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain why exchanging the percentage and quantity preserves the result, then apply this to mental calculations.

questions.mappingNote: Finding a percentage of a quantity is directly assessed in all eight calculations; part a explains the commutative multiplication underlying that method.
questions.methodNote: Pages 1–2 explain percentages as fractions of 100. Page 3, Example 5, calculates percentages using convenient fractions or multiplication. The supplied demonstration in question 10 introduces exchanging the percentage and quantity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explain why exchanging the percentage and quantity preserves the result, then apply this to mental calculations.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover the total represented by four averaged scores, interpret score bounds and reverse the five-test average to find the required final score.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) combines four scores represented by their average with one new score. Parts (b) and (c) use the same calculation with fifth-test bounds of 100% and 0%. Part (d) equates the five-test average to 85% and solves for the missing score. The closest catalogue skill is expressing a quantity as a percentage; solving a linear equation is secondary.
questions.methodNote: Page 2, Example 4, combines percentage averages by multiplying each average by its number of students, adding the totals and dividing by the combined count. Apply the same total-score method to five tests. Page 3, Example 6, supports solving for an unknown amount using an equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines an existing average with a fifth score, interprets maximum and minimum scores, and reverses the average calculation.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise each stated amount as a known percentage of the whole and directly apply the taught scaling to 100%.

questions.mappingNote: Every part supplies a percentage of an unknown whole and its value, directly matching Example 6. The unitary-method-percentages skill is the closest catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Page 3, Example 6, teaches recovering an unknown amount by scaling a known percentage to 100%, or by solving a fractional percentage equation. These solutions use the scaling method through 1%.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover an unknown whole from a given percentage using the method taught in Example 6.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate percentage coefficients into decimals, then solve equations; the hardest part requires expanding brackets and collecting unknown terms from both sides.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses solving a linear equation after converting its percentage coefficient. The closest catalogue skill is solve-linear-2-step; part d extends this to x on both sides.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 establishes percentage notation and decimal equivalence. Page 3, Example 6 Method 2, converts a percentage of an unknown amount into an algebraic equation and isolates the unknown. Apply this method with inverse operations; expand and collect terms in part d.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert percentage coefficients and solve linear equations, including an equation with x on both sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Model changing class membership with a percentage equation, then solve for the original class size.

questions.mappingNote: Question 14 assesses the same changing-membership model as Example 7, with five members joining instead of fifteen leaving. Linear-equation solving is the most advanced directly assessed skill; percentage representation supplies the model.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 on page 3 continues on page 4: define the original total and subgroup, express the changed subgroup as a fraction of the changed total, substitute the original percentage, multiply by 100 and solve the linear equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model changing class membership with a percentage equation, then solve for the original class size.

classification.difficultyReason: Form an equation linking percentage counts before and after students leave, accounting for the changed class total.

questions.mappingNote: Question 15 requires an equation for the original class size; the changed total and changed black-haired count must both be represented. The closest catalogue skill is solving a linear equation, supported by percentage-of-quantity knowledge.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 defines percentages as fractions of 100. Page 3 Example 6, Method 2, represents a percentage of an unknown amount algebraically. Example 7 supplies the analogous situation of students leaving and changing the percentage.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form an equation linking percentage counts before and after students leave, accounting for the changed class total.

classification.difficultyReason: Weight each class average by its student count and divide the combined score total by the combined count, following the taught example.

questions.mappingNote: Question 16 directly adapts Example 4 with class sizes 10 and 15 and averages 60% and 80%. Percentage-of-quantity is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 weights each class percentage average by its number of students, adds the weighted totals and divides by the combined number of students.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines two percentage averages using different class sizes as weights.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer the total from the complementary percentage before expressing the red lollies as a percentage.

questions.mappingNote: The non-blue complement supplies the known percentage and count; the final task directly assesses expressing the red count as a percentage of the inferred whole.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 Example 6 finds an unknown total from a known percentage using fraction arithmetic or the unitary method. Page 2 expresses a part as a percentage of the whole.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer the total from the complementary percentage before expressing the red lollies as a percentage.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer fuel consumed from two tank readings, scale the observed distance to the remaining fuel and compare that range with the remaining journey.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task is a constant fuel-use rate problem expressed using tank percentages. The answer evidence uses the same proportional scaling and compares the available distance with the remaining journey.
questions.methodNote: Page 3, Example 6 Method 1, scales known percentage amounts proportionally. Apply the same method to fuel and distance: 15% of the tank gives 165 km, so 45% gives three times that distance.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer fuel used, scale the remaining fuel to a travel distance, and compare it with the distance still required.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate the percentage for sale within each property category, then combine their contributions to the whole.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed operation is finding percentages of quantities in two disjoint categories; percentage-of-quantity is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 calculates a percentage of a number by multiplying by the percentage expressed as a fraction or decimal. Apply this to each category’s percentage of the whole and add the contributions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate the percentage for sale within each property category, then combine their contributions to the whole.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires applying two percentages successively to nested groups.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is finding percentages of quantities within nested groups; it does not assess percentage change.
questions.methodNote: Page 3, Example 5 Method 2, calculates a percentage by multiplying the quantity by the percentage as a fraction or decimal. Apply this first to all students, then to the boys.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires applying two percentages successively to nested groups.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires expressing changed numbers of boys and students algebraically, then solving a percentage equation.

questions.mappingNote: Question 21 uses the same changing-class-composition method, with five boys joining instead of leaving. The assessed percentage compares boys with the whole class.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 defines the original class size and number of boys, expresses the changed boy count as a fraction of the changed class size, substitutes the original percentage and solves the resulting linear equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires expressing changed numbers of boys and students algebraically, then solving a percentage equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Form and solve an equation involving changing numbers of boys and students.

questions.mappingNote: Question 22 uses the same departing-boys structure as Example 7. Solving the resulting linear equation is the most advanced directly assessed step.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 begins on PDF page 3 and continues on page 4. Define the original total and boys, express the remaining boys as a fraction of the remaining total, substitute the original percentage, multiply by 100 and solve.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form and solve an equation involving changing numbers of boys and students.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer the percentage of capacity removed from the initial empty percentage and final full percentage, then find the whole.

questions.mappingNote: The barrel's initial fullness is the complement of its empty percentage. The removed volume is the difference between initial and final fullness; apply the taught unitary method to that percentage.
questions.methodNote: Page 3, Example 6, teaches finding an unknown whole from a known percentage using proportional percentage steps.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer the percentage of capacity removed from the initial empty percentage and final full percentage, then find the whole.

classification.difficultyReason: Model a mixture using the total volume and the ethanol contributed by two different concentrations.

questions.mappingNote: Apply these percentage methods to each solution's ethanol contribution and equate their sum to the ethanol in the final mixture. The closest catalogue skill covers practical mixture problems.
questions.methodNote: Page 3, Examples 5 and 6, calculate a percentage by multiplication and express a percentage of an unknown amount as an equation. Page 2, Example 4, combines contributions from groups with different percentages.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model a mixture using the total volume and the ethanol contributed by two different concentrations.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the taught increase or decrease multiplier for each explicit instruction and multiply the given quantity.

questions.mappingNote: All assigned parts assess single percentage changes. Page 8's reverse-percentage and percentage-change methods are unnecessary here.
questions.methodNote: Use 1 plus the decimal percentage for an increase and 1 minus it for a decrease. Single-change rules are taught on pages 6–7.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Each part requires one directly specified percentage increase or decrease.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct percentage changes using decimal multipliers, including small fractional percentages.

questions.mappingNote: Every assigned part directly applies one percentage multiplier to its original amount; percentage-multiplier is the closest directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1–4 establish multiplication by 1 + P/100 for increases and 1 - P/100 for decreases; Examples 2 and 4 demonstrate decimal percentage multipliers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct percentage changes using decimal multipliers, including small fractional percentages.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the percentage represented by the final price and reverse the percentage change.

questions.mappingNote: Each of parts a–f gives a final price and one percentage change and asks for the original price, directly matching Example 5. Parts b and d use the corresponding decrease multipliers taught on page 7.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 establish increase and decrease multipliers. Page 8, Example 5 Method 2, identifies the final percentage, forms a multiplier equation and divides to recover the original price.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the percentage represented by the final price and reverse the percentage change.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the price difference, divide by the original price and express the result as a percentage with the stated direction of change.

questions.mappingNote: Every part supplies original and final prices and directly assesses percentage change. Use the positive magnitude of the change and state increase or decrease.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 defines percentage change as change in value divided by original value, multiplied by 100%. Example 6 demonstrates substitution, simplification and identification of an increase. Pages 6–7 establish increases and decreases.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of the taught percentage-change formula to given original and final prices.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply two successive percentage multipliers and calculate the overall change relative to the original amount.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses repeated percentage change: (a) two 50% increases; (b) a 10% increase and 50% decrease; (c) a 5% increase and 10% decrease; (d) two 10% decreases; (e) two 10% increases; (f) 20% and 10% increases; (g) a 10% decrease and 20% increase.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 teach multiplication by 1 + P/100 for increases and 1 - P/100 for decreases. Page 8 teaches change divided by original value, multiplied by 100%. Apply the two multipliers successively, then compare the final amount with the original.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply two successive percentage multipliers and calculate the overall change relative to the original amount.

classification.difficultyReason: Extends three numerical calculations to a general algebraic proof.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c apply successive changes to a monetary amount; part d generalises the same multiplier method. Repeated percentage change is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: The inspected examples derive increase and decrease multipliers as 1 + P/100 and 1 - P/100. Apply these successively, then expand their product for the proof.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extends three numerical calculations to a general algebraic proof.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine successive change multipliers, then reframe two equal increases as equal factors of the combined multiplier and convert each factor back to a percentage.

questions.mappingNote: Part a interprets 1.44 as a 44% increase. Part b recognises 1.44 as 1.2 × 1.2, giving two 20% increases; this agrees with the teacher's method.
questions.methodNote: Use the taught increase multiplier 1 + P/100 and decrease multiplier 1 - P/100. Multiply successive multipliers and interpret the result relative to 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines successive multipliers and identifies two equal increases giving the same result.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the decrease multipliers and recognise that two equal decreases require the positive equal factor of their product, then interpret its percentage decrease.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) multiplies successive decrease multipliers; part (b) identifies equal multipliers whose product is the same. Repeated percentage change is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: The teaching derives percentage-change multipliers: multiply by 1 minus the percentage expressed as a decimal for a decrease.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine successive decreases and identify two equal multipliers giving the same result.

classification.difficultyReason: The restoring percentage must use the changed amount as its base.

questions.mappingNote: Each part requires reversing a percentage change and expressing the restoring difference as a percentage of the changed amount; reverse-percentage-problems is the closest catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1–4 teach percentage multipliers; Example 6 calculates change divided by the starting value times 100%. For the restoring change, the changed amount is the starting value.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The restoring percentage must use the changed amount as its base.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify a decrease, subtract the final count from the original and apply the taught percentage-change formula using 160 as the base.

questions.mappingNote: The original count is 160 and the final count is 116; the directly assessed skill is calculating percentage change.
questions.methodNote: Page 8, Example 6, calculates percentage change by dividing the change by the original amount and multiplying by 100%. For a decrease, use the positive decrease and state its direction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the taught percentage-change formula to an original and final count.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate the original and new square areas before expressing their difference as a percentage of the original area.

questions.mappingNote: Apply that method to square areas rather than side lengths: the original area is 4 square centimetres and the new area is 9 square centimetres.
questions.methodNote: Page 8, Example 6, Method 1 calculates percentage change as the change divided by the original value, multiplied by 100%.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate the original and new square areas before expressing their difference as a percentage of the original area.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the new side length from the area before reversing its percentage increase.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the square-area relationship to obtain the new side, then reverse the 25% increase using the taught multiplier method.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 teach percentage multipliers. Page 8, Example 5, teaches finding an original amount by identifying the new percentage and dividing by its multiplier.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the new side length from the area before reversing its percentage increase.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines two side-length percentage multipliers and interprets their product as an area increase.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the taught multiplier method to each side, multiply the resulting factors through the rectangle area formula, then interpret 1.56 as a 56% increase.
questions.methodNote: The inspected examples calculate percentage increases using multipliers of the form 1 + P/100.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines two side-length percentage multipliers and interprets their product as an area increase.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the percentage increase to area rather than side length, recover the new side using a square root and subtract the original side.

questions.mappingNote: Percentage multipliers are directly assessed through the 44% area increase; finding a square side from its area is the supporting step.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1 and 2 teach increasing a quantity using the multiplier 1 + P/100. Apply 1.44 to the original square area, take its positive square root, and subtract the original side length.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply a percentage multiplier to area, find the new square side length, then calculate the increase.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent boys as 120% of girls, then use the combined class total to find the original quantity.

questions.mappingNote: The girls are the reference quantity; boys are 120% of that quantity. Adding both groups gives 2.2x = 33, a reverse percentage problem.
questions.methodNote: A 20% increase corresponds to multiplication by 1.2. Example 5 permits finding an unknown original quantity by forming and solving an equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent boys as 120% of girls, then use the combined class total to find the original quantity.

classification.difficultyReason: Express the girls as 60% of the boys, then use the combined class total to find the boys.

questions.mappingNote: Girls are 60% of boys, so the total is 160% of the boys. The teacher solution explicitly uses x + 0.6x = 32 and obtains 20 boys.
questions.methodNote: Percentage decreases use the multiplier 1 minus the percentage as a decimal. Example 5 also teaches forming an equation in the original amount and dividing to solve.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express the girls as 60% of the boys, then use the combined class total to find the boys.

classification.difficultyReason: Relates two changing student counts using different percentage bases and solves for the original counts.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task reconstructs original counts from percentage relationships before and after students leave; reverse-percentage-problems is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use percentage multipliers 1.2 and 0.75, then solve an equation for the original number of girls. Example 5 supports representing an original quantity by x and solving a multiplier equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Relates two changing student counts using different percentage bases and solves for the original counts.

classification.difficultyReason: Model reversed digits using place value and percentage multipliers, then use integer digit restrictions both to isolate a valid number and prove impossibility.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess percentage multipliers in digit-reversal equations. Part (a) determines and checks the number; part (b) proves impossibility using integer digits. Teacher page 10 supplies the corresponding place-value method.
questions.methodNote: Use the taught percentage-increase multiplier, then solve the resulting equation as in the algebraic method of Example 5. Represent a two-digit number by its place values and apply digit constraints.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate reversed digits into percentage equations and use integer digit constraints to establish uniqueness or impossibility.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a three-digit reversal equation, derive parity and digit bounds, and systematically exhaust valid digit combinations to establish all solutions.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed percentage method is the 1.75 multiplier; digit constraints extend the problem beyond routine percentage calculation.
questions.methodNote: Use the taught percentage multiplier: increasing by P% multiplies the original by 1+P/100. Represent digits by place value, form an equation and test the permitted digit values, as in the teacher solution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate reversed digits into a percentage equation and exhaust the possible digit values.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires expressing a digit transformation algebraically and solving for the original number using a percentage multiplier.

questions.mappingNote: Reverse percentage problems is the closest catalogue match because the original number is unknown and its transformed value is 120% of that number.
questions.methodNote: The teaching establishes percentage multipliers and uses algebra to find an original amount. Express the digit change through place value, then use the 1.2 multiplier.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires expressing a digit transformation algebraically and solving for the original number using a percentage multiplier.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines successive multipliers, constructs button sequences and proves an unattainable percentage.

questions.mappingNote: Repeated percentage change is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill: parts (a)–(e) combine multipliers, part (f) reasons about attainable products and part (g) applies commutativity.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 teach percentage multipliers. The permanent examples within question 21 explicitly teach multiplying successive copy-size percentages. The teacher solution uses fractional multipliers and prime factors for the impossibility proof.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines successive multipliers, constructs button sequences and proves an unattainable percentage.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive the perimeter contribution of an attached square, then translate its side-length ratio into an area percentage.

questions.mappingNote: Percentage change is the directly assessed result; the attached-square geometry supplies the change in area.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 establish percentage-change multipliers; page 8 defines percentage change as change divided by original value times 100%. Apply these to the perimeter gain and then the added area.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derive the perimeter contribution of an attached square, then translate its side-length ratio into an area percentage.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate changes to individual digits into a numerical increase, solve a reverse percentage equation and establish impossibility using integer values.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts require finding an original number from its percentage increase; the digit transformation supplies the known increase. Reverse percentage problems is the closest existing skill, with percentage multipliers and algebraic translation supporting the task.
questions.methodNote: Percentage increases use the multiplier 1+P/100. Example 5 also solves for an original amount using a percentage equation. The teacher solution for 23 expands place values to obtain x+111, then equates the new-to-original ratio to 13/10 or 7/5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate changes to individual digits into a numerical increase, solve a reverse percentage equation and establish impossibility using integer values.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplify two- and three-term integer ratios using a common factor.

questions.mappingNote: Each of 1(a)–1(h) directly assesses the integer-ratio simplification rule on page 12. The three-term parts also use that page's definition of ratios comparing three or more quantities.
questions.methodNote: Divide every term of a ratio by the same positive common factor, continuing until the integer terms have no common factor greater than one.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplify two- and three-term integer ratios using a common factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Clear fractional and mixed-number terms using common denominators, then simplify to lowest whole-number terms.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts assess the fractional-ratio method explicitly demonstrated in Example 1(b).
questions.methodNote: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions, express all ratio terms over a common denominator, clear it, and divide by any remaining common factor.
